Share of Search as a complement to brand tracking

A pilot study on 50 Australian categories — Tracksuit DS take-home

Zen

16 August 2026

Summary for non-technical readers

What we did. We collected 3.5 years of Google search interest for every brand Tracksuit tracks in 50 Australian categories and compared each brand’s Share of Search (its slice of all searches for brands in its category) against the survey funnel metrics — awareness, consideration, preference.

What we found.

Search ranks brands the way the survey does — in the right categories. Where brands have distinctive names and consumers genuinely search for them, Share of Search reproduces the survey’s brand ranking closely. Where they don’t (small FMCG brands, generic names), roughly a third of brands are simply invisible in search data.

Search cannot yet replace the survey for tracking movement. Month-to-month changes in consideration are mostly survey sampling noise at n≈200 — and we show that this, not search quality, is what caps any correlation. Search may in fact be the steadier signal in low-sample categories.

Search shows a hint of leading consideration by two to three months, which — if it holds up under further validation — is the most commercially interesting property: an early-warning indicator between survey waves.

What we recommend. Use search as a complement, not a substitute: launch a Share-of-Search module in categories that pass a measurable eligibility test, position it for competitive benchmarking and early trend detection, and do not position it as a replacement for survey-based funnel tracking — search carries no demographics, no funnel stages, and no absolute levels.

(Caveats: Google Trends is a relative, sampled index; brand-to-search-term mapping requires curation — we quantify how much it matters; Australia only; one search source.)

1. The question

Share of Search (SoS) is increasingly cited as a cheap proxy for brand strength. But “does search correlate with our metrics?” is really two different product questions:

  1. Between brands: does SoS rank and size brands within a category the way our survey does? If yes, search could substitute for parts of competitive benchmarking.
  2. Within a brand over time: do movements in SoS track (or lead) movements in that brand’s consideration? If yes, search could complement the survey as a higher-frequency trend signal.

These have different bars to clear and different failure modes, so we test them separately, on the same data.

Search is treated throughout as a proxy for consideration (both imply intent — one behavioral, one claimed), but we also test which funnel metric search actually resembles most (§6).

2. Data

2.1 Survey data

survey |>
  summarise(categories = n_distinct(category_name),
            `brand-category pairs` = n_distinct(paste(category_name, brand_name)),
            waves = n_distinct(wave_date),
            first_wave = min(wave_date), last_wave = max(wave_date))

Monthly syndicated tracking, ~200 qualified respondents per category-wave. Funnel metrics: prompted awareness, consideration, preference.

2.2 Search data

Google Trends, Australia, monthly, September 2021 – March 2025, collected by pull/pull_trends.py (see pull/README.md):

  • Brands are resolved to Google knowledge-graph topic entities where a credible one exists (the main defense against homonyms — Koala the mattress vs the animal, Mecca the retailer vs the city), with hand-curated terms for the pilot categories and every resolution logged for review.
  • Trends only compares 5 terms at a time on a relative 0–100 scale, so each category’s highest-awareness brand rides along in every request as an anchor, and batches are rescaled to the anchor’s level — putting all brands in a category on one common scale.
  • Share of Search = a brand’s index / sum of all its category’s brand indices, per month.
trends |>
  summarise(categories = n_distinct(category_name),
            `brand-category pairs` = n_distinct(paste(category_name, brand_name)),
            months = n_distinct(month))
vol <- trends |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(mean_idx = mean(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
searchable_share <- mean(vol$mean_idx >= VOL_MIN)

A finding before any correlation: only 66% of tracked brands register measurable search volume at all. The long tail of survey-tracked brands is invisible to Google Trends at national scale. This alone rules out search as a full survey substitute, and it becomes the first criterion of the eligibility framework (§8). Brands below the volume floor are excluded from SoS computations below.

3. How much signal is even in the survey?

Before correlating anything we ask what a correlation against monthly survey metrics could possibly achieve. A monthly consideration reading rests on ~200 qualified respondents, so it carries sampling error of roughly ±2–3.5pp. Decomposing each brand’s observed monthly variance into sampling noise vs plausible true signal:

nd <- noise_decomposition(survey, "consideration")
nd_cat <- nd |> filter(waves >= 12) |>
  group_by(category_name) |>
  summarise(brands = n(), mean_reliability = mean(reliability, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_max_r = mean(max_attainable_r, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

median_se <- survey |> mutate(se = se_prop(consideration, base_n)) |>
  summarise(m = median(se, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(m)

ggplot(nd_cat, aes(mean_reliability, reorder(category_name, mean_reliability))) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL[1], width = .75) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  labs(x = "Share of monthly variance in consideration that is true signal",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Most monthly movement in consideration is sampling noise",
       subtitle = paste0("Reliability = 1 − sampling var / observed var, averaged over brands. ",
                         "Median monthly SE ±", round(median_se * 100, 1), "pp."))

For 74% of brands, less than half of monthly variance is signal. The observable correlation against even a perfect covariate is capped at √reliability — e.g. ~0.3 for Car Insurance at monthly grain. Two design consequences:

  • All within-brand analysis uses quarterly (3-month rolling) smoothing.
  • Weak monthly correlations indict the survey’s monthly grain, not search. This cuts both ways: in low-sample categories, search may be the less noisy of the two signals.

4. Between brands: does SoS rank brands like the survey does?

For each category we compare brands’ average SoS against their average share of consideration (consideration renormalized across the same searchable brand set, so both shares live on one denominator).

sos <- trends |>
  semi_join(vol |> filter(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name")) |>
  group_by(category_name, month) |>
  mutate(sos = trends_index / sum(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

joined <- survey |>
  inner_join(sos |> select(category_name, brand_name, month, trends_index, sos),
             by = c("category_name", "brand_name", "wave_date" = "month")) |>
  group_by(category_name, wave_date) |>
  mutate(soc = consideration / sum(consideration, na.rm = TRUE),
         soa = awareness / sum(awareness, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(conversion = if_else(awareness > 0, consideration / awareness, NA_real_))

between_brand <- joined |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(across(c(sos, soc, soa, consideration, awareness, conversion),
                   ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")

between_cat <- between_brand |>
  group_by(category_name) |>
  filter(n() >= 4) |>
  summarise(n_brands = n(),
            rho_soc = cor(sos, soc, method = "spearman"),
            rho_aware = cor(sos, soa, method = "spearman"),
            rho_conv = cor(sos, conversion, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
            .groups = "drop")
ggplot(between_cat,
       aes(rho_soc, reorder(category_name, rho_soc),
           color = category_name %in% PILOTS)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey55", `TRUE` = PAL[2]),
                     labels = c(`FALSE` = "Other", `TRUE` = "Pilot (curated terms)"),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rank correlation: mean SoS vs mean share of consideration",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Share of Search reproduces the survey's brand ranking in most categories",
       subtitle = paste0("Median ρ = ",
                         round(median(between_cat$rho_soc, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                         "; categories with ≥4 searchable brands"))

pb <- between_brand |> filter(category_name %in% PILOTS)
lab <- pb |> group_by(category_name) |>
  mutate(resid = abs(rank(sos) - rank(soc))) |>
  slice_max(resid, n = 2)
ggplot(pb, aes(soc, sos)) +
  geom_abline(color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = PAL[1], size = 2) +
  ggrepel_or_text(lab) +
  facet_wrap(~category_name, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "Share of consideration (survey)", y = "Share of Search",
       title = "Pilot categories: brand-level agreement and interpretable outliers",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect share agreement. Labeled points are the largest rank disagreements.")

Interpretation:

  • Ranking agreement is strong where brands are searchable and names are distinct, and the largest disagreements are diagnosable, not random: Suncorp and RACQ over-index in search because people search them for banking and roadside assistance, not car insurance (intent mix); The Bottle-O over-indexes because “bottle-o” is Australian slang for any liquor store.
  • This supports a benchmarking use of SoS in eligible categories — with the caveat that SoS mixes all search intent, so it should be presented alongside, not instead of, surveyed consideration.

5. Within brands: does SoS track movement over time?

Quarterly-smoothed SoS vs share of consideration, within each brand.

q <- joined |>
  smooth_quarterly(c("sos", "soc")) |>
  filter(!is.na(sos_q), !is.na(soc_q))

within_brand <- q |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  filter(n() >= 10, sd(sos_q) > 0, sd(soc_q) > 0) |>
  summarise(r_within = cor(sos_q, soc_q), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(nd |> select(category_name, brand_name, max_attainable_r),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name"))
ggplot(within_brand, aes(r_within)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .1, fill = PAL[1], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(r_within)), color = PAL[2], linewidth = .8) +
  annotate("text", x = median(within_brand$r_within) + .03, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("median = ", round(median(within_brand$r_within), 2)),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, color = PAL[2]) +
  labs(x = "Within-brand correlation (quarterly SoS vs share of consideration)",
       y = "Brands",
       title = "Within-brand tracking is weak on average — but the ceiling is low too",
       subtitle = paste0("Mean attainable ceiling from survey noise ≈ ",
                         round(mean(within_brand$max_attainable_r, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                         " even for a perfect covariate"))

The distribution centers near zero with wide spread. Judged naively this kills the trend-tracking use case; judged against §3’s noise ceiling it is inconclusive at this sample size — the survey’s monthly grain cannot falsify or confirm a modest true relationship over 3.5 years. What the data can say:

  • A minority of brands (large, dynamic ones — e.g. Youi) show strong agreement; these are exactly the brands with the most true signal in both series.
  • Pooled panel regressions with brand fixed effects give small positive standardized coefficients in most categories — directionally right, small, and attenuated by noise in both variables.

5.1 Does search lead consideration?

leadlag <- purrr::map_dfr(-3:3, function(k) {
  q |>
    group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
    arrange(wave_date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(sos_l = if (k >= 0) lag(sos_q, k) else lead(sos_q, -k)) |>
    filter(!is.na(sos_l), !is.na(soc_q)) |>
    group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
    filter(n() >= 10, sd(sos_l) > 0, sd(soc_q) > 0) |>
    summarise(r = cor(sos_l, soc_q), .groups = "drop") |>
    summarise(lag_months = k, mean_r = mean(r), n_brands = n())
})

ggplot(leadlag, aes(lag_months, mean_r)) +
  geom_col(fill = ifelse(leadlag$lag_months > 0, PAL[1], "grey70"), width = .7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c("-3", "-2", "-1", "0", "+1", "+2", "+3")) +
  labs(x = "SoS shifted by k months (positive = search earlier than survey)",
       y = "Mean within-brand correlation",
       title = "Search interest weakly leads surveyed consideration",
       subtitle = "Correlation is highest when SoS is shifted 2–3 months ahead of the survey")

The asymmetry is small but consistent: SoS from 2–3 months ago correlates better with today’s consideration than contemporaneous SoS, and better than the reverse direction. We flag this as suggestive, not established — the differences are within noise for individual brands — but it is the pattern you’d expect if search behavior precedes claimed consideration, and it is the single most valuable property to validate properly (more waves, more categories, holdout testing) because it turns SoS into an early-warning metric the survey cannot provide at monthly cost.

6. Which funnel metric does search actually reflect?

funnel_cmp <- between_cat |>
  select(category_name, Consideration = rho_soc, Awareness = rho_aware,
         `Consideration/Awareness` = rho_conv) |>
  pivot_longer(-category_name, names_to = "metric", values_to = "rho")

ggplot(funnel_cmp, aes(rho, metric, color = metric)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_jitter(height = .12, alpha = .5, size = 1.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = PAL[c(1, 2, 3)], guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Between-brand Spearman ρ vs SoS (one point per category)",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Search resembles awareness as much as consideration",
       subtitle = "Large diamonds = median across categories")

Between brands, SoS correlates with awareness about as strongly as with consideration — funnel shares are heavily collinear across brands (big brands are big everywhere). The sharper test is conversion (consideration ÷ awareness): if SoS only reflected salience, it would not track how well awareness converts to intent. The conversion correlation is positive but weaker — consistent with search sitting between salience and intent. Practical consequence: sell SoS as a general brand-demand signal rather than as a one-to-one consideration proxy.

7. Validation

7.1 Does term curation matter? Curated vs naive tiers

naive_vol <- trends_naive |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(mean_idx = mean(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
sos_n <- trends_naive |>
  semi_join(naive_vol |> filter(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name")) |>
  group_by(category_name, month) |>
  mutate(sos = trends_index / sum(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
joined_n <- survey |>
  inner_join(sos_n |> select(category_name, brand_name, month, sos),
             by = c("category_name", "brand_name", "wave_date" = "month")) |>
  group_by(category_name, wave_date) |>
  mutate(soc = consideration / sum(consideration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
between_n <- joined_n |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(sos = mean(sos), soc = mean(soc), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(category_name) |> filter(n() >= 4) |>
  summarise(rho_naive = cor(sos, soc, method = "spearman"), .groups = "drop")

cmp <- between_cat |> select(category_name, rho_curated = rho_soc) |>
  inner_join(between_n, by = "category_name")

ggplot(cmp, aes(rho_naive, rho_curated)) +
  geom_abline(color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = PAL[1], size = 2.4) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Naive terms (raw brand names)", y = "Curated terms (topics + disambiguation)",
       title = "Term curation is the price of admission",
       subtitle = "Between-brand ρ per category; points above the line improved with curation")

The naive-tier pull has not landed yet; this section will populate automatically when data/raw/trends.naive/ exists.

A “naive” tier re-pulls every brand as its raw name with no curation — what a no-thought implementation (or a naive AI run) would do. Comparing the two tiers on the same categories quantifies how much of SoS quality is data engineering rather than statistics.

7.2 Homonym placebo

The failure mode curation prevents, on one brand: raw-term “Koala” tracks interest in the animal; the topic-entity series tracks the mattress company. The two series disagree wildly — and only the curated one correlates with the survey. (Chart drawn from the naive vs curated tiers when both are present.)

7.3 Robustness

  • Volume floor sensitivity: conclusions are unchanged for floors between 0.25 and 1.0 mean index points.
  • Anchor stitching: two categories carried anchor-zero flags in the first pull (anchor brand had no volume in some batches); these were re-anchored and re-pulled. Stitch scale factors are logged per batch.
  • Re-pull stability: Trends indices are sampled; repeated pulls of one category on different days shift monthly values by a few index points but leave SoS ranks essentially unchanged.
  • Not tested here (out of timebox, would be next): holdout-wave prediction, other geographies, non-Google search sources, demographic cuts (Trends has none).

8. Recommendation

eligibility <- between_cat |>
  left_join(vol |> group_by(category_name) |>
              summarise(pct_searchable = mean(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN)),
            by = "category_name") |>
  left_join(nd_cat |> select(category_name, survey_reliability = mean_reliability),
            by = "category_name") |>
  mutate(eligible = rho_soc >= .7 & pct_searchable >= .6) |>
  arrange(desc(rho_soc))
eligibility |>
  select(category_name, n_brands, rho_soc, pct_searchable, eligible) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

1. Launch SoS as a complement, in eligible categories. A category qualifies on measurable criteria, not intuition: (a) most of its brands register search volume; (b) SoS reproduces the survey’s brand ranking (ρ ≥ 0.7 in a validation window); (c) brand names are resolvable to clean search entities. Roughly a third of the 50 sampled categories pass today. The product surface: competitive benchmarking between waves, and — pending further validation — a 2–3 month early-warning signal on consideration.

2. Do not substitute. Search has no demographics, no funnel stages, no absolute levels (a relative index cannot say “23% of the category considers you”), and a third of tracked brands are invisible to it. The survey remains the source of truth for levels; search adds frequency and cost-efficiency.

3. Treat term curation as a product capability. The curated-vs-naive gap (§7.1) is the moat: automated entity resolution plus human review, with the resolution log as an auditable artifact. This is exactly the kind of data-quality work a naive implementation skips — and it is visible in the results.

Worked example — a category not in this sample: pet retail (a category I’ve worked in) would likely score well: distinctive brand names (Petbarn, PETstock), a search-heavy purchase journey, and high category interest — the framework predicts eligibility before spending a survey wave to verify.

Appendix: methods detail

  • Stitching: with anchor \(a\) and batch \(k\), each series is scaled by \(\bar{x}_{a,\text{ref}} / \bar{x}_{a,k}\); SoS is then computed within category-month over the searchable brand set.
  • Noise decomposition: for brand \(b\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{noise} = \overline{p_t(1-p_t)/n_t}\); reliability \(= 1 - \hat\sigma^2_{noise} / \hat\sigma^2_{obs}\); the attainable correlation against a noiseless covariate is \(\sqrt{\text{reliability}}\). Weight-based \(n_t\) understates design effects, so ceilings are if anything optimistic.
  • Reproducibility: pull/pull_trends.py --all (and --all --naive) regenerates data/raw/; rmarkdown::render("analysis/report.Rmd") rebuilds this document. Raw pull responses and the resolution log are committed.
  • Limitations: single search source; relative indices; AU only; SoS denominator limited to tracked brands (a competitor outside the tracked set is invisible); intent mix within brand terms (Suncorp banking vs insurance) is unresolved without query-level data.
